turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Totally get it; roses come with a lot of jargon. Here are the main choices in very simple terms:

Type of rose (shape and use)
Bush / shrub roses: These are rounded plants that stay in a “bush” shape. Great for most gardens and beginners.
Climbing roses: Long canes you tie to a trellis, fence, or arbor. They do not cling by themselves; you attach them as they grow.
Groundcover / landscape roses: Low, spreading plants that cover an area. Good for slopes, borders, or filling space.
Size Every rose on our site lists a height and width in feet.
Smaller (around 2–3 feet): Good for pots or small spaces.
Medium (3–5 feet): Typical garden bush size.
Large / tall (5+ feet or climbers): Better for fences, walls, or bigger beds.
Bloom style
Hybrid tea style: One big flower per stem, like florist roses. Good for cutting and vases.
Clusters: Many blooms together in bunches. This often gives a fuller look in the garden.
Bloom frequency
Repeat blooming: Blooms, rests, then blooms again several times in the season.
Continuous blooming: Keeps flowers coming almost nonstop in the season (with short rests).
Fragrance On each product you will see “fragrance” noted.
Strong fragrance: Great if scent is very important to you.
Light or moderate: Nice scent but not overwhelming.
Sun and climate
Sun: Roses need full sun, which means 6 or more hours of direct sunlight each day.
Hardiness zone: At the top of our website you can pick your zone (for example, Zone 5, Zone 8). That helps show roses that will handle your winter temperatures.
How our roses arrive
All our roses are own-root and come in 1-gallon containers with soil.
They are defoliated for shipping, so they often arrive without leaves or buds; they leaf out once planted and cared for.

Gentle fertilizer
A mild, easy fertilizer helps new roses establish without overdoing it.
Founders Fish Fertilizer (our fish fertilizer) is great for a rose’s first year and can be applied every 4 weeks during the growing season.
Mulch

Hold moisture
Keep roots cooler
Suppress weeds

How do I use it properly the very first time?

You’re so close to actually growing your first rose, which is exciting. Let’s walk through what to do the very first time, step by step.

I’ll explain this as “Day 1 with your new rose.”

When the box arrives
Open the box right away.
Take the rose out and set the container outdoors in a bright spot that gets some sun.
Give it a good, slow drink of water until water runs out the drainage holes.
Decide if you’re planting in the ground or a container
Either way, plant within about 2 weeks of arrival.
Only plant in the ground if your weather is frost-safe (after your last spring frost or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost).
If it’s not planting time yet, move the rose from the shipping pot into a larger container (about 10" across or bigger) and keep it outdoors, not indoors.
How to plant in the ground (first time)
Pick a spot with at least 6 hours of direct sun and soil that drains well (no standing water after rain).
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and deep enough so that when the rose sits in it, the soil level in the pot matches the ground level.
Mix some organic matter into your native soil if you have heavy clay or very sandy soil (compost or aged manure works well).
Gently remove the rose from its pot, loosen the roots a bit with your fingers, and set it in the center of the hole.
Backfill with your soil mix, gently firming it so there are no big air pockets, keeping the base of the plant at ground level.
Water deeply to settle the soil.
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch around the plant, but keep it a couple of inches away from the base so it does not sit right against the stems.
If you’re using starter products (like a bundle or fertilizer)
For soil amendments like compost or aged manure: mix them into the soil you put back in the hole or use as a light top layer after planting.
For a gentle liquid fertilizer like fish fertilizer: mix it with water at the labeled rate and water the plant with it after planting, then repeat every few weeks during the growing season.
Skip strong granular fertilizers in the very first season unless the product directions specifically say they are safe for new roses; too much can burn young roots.
First weeks of care
Water deeply 2–3 times per week at first (more often in very hot, dry weather, less often if it’s cool and rainy). The goal is moist soil, not soggy.
Watch for new leaves and stems; that is your main sign it’s settling in.
When blooms fade, you can “deadhead,” which means cutting off the spent flower just above a leaf with 5–7 leaflets. This encourages more blooms.
One important rule
Keep the rose outdoors. Roses need outdoor conditions and a winter rest period. Growing them indoors long term is not healthy for them.
